solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Man with knife, sharper, cutting meat about

indicators.note: a blade that cuts goes into the middle of something, so one piece is set inside the other
to bring something about is to turn it round, so these letters run the other way

parts.note: ham is a kind of meat
a sharper is a swindler or card cheat

explanation.surface: A knife-wielding con man slicing up a joint of meat.
explanation.walkthrough: Macheath, Mack the Knife, is the highwayman antihero of The Beggar's Opera and The Threepenny Opera. 'Sharper' looks like a comparative of sharp, fitting the knife, but is a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Mack the Knife is the nickname of the highwayman character in Gay's and Brecht's ballad operas.

clue.text: Opening letter scandal, as it were, is a gem

parts.note: the first letter of the alphabet
after Watergate, -gate is tacked on to name any scandal

explanation.surface: A leaked letter that starts a scandal turns out to be a gem.
explanation.walkthrough: 'As it were' admits that GATE is only a scandal by way of the suffix, as in Watergate or Partygate.
explanation.definitionFit: Agate is a banded variety of chalcedony, a semi-precious stone used in jewellery.

clue.text: Useful foreign character, told to be race official

indicators.note: something told is spoken, so it is the sound of the words that counts here

parts.note: handy means useful
kappa is a letter of the Greek alphabet

explanation.surface: A helpful foreigner is said to be in line for a job at the racecourse.
explanation.walkthrough: HANDY KAPPA said aloud gives HANDICAPPER. 'Foreign character' is a Greek letter, not a person from abroad.
explanation.definitionFit: A handicapper assigns weights to horses in a handicap race so that all runners have an equal chance.

clue.text: Flying stunts, not at these exercises

indicators.note: saying 'not' these letters tells us to leave them out of the word

parts.note: loops and rolls performed by aircraft
taken as written; these letters are removed

explanation.surface: Stunt flying is not what goes on at a keep-fit class.
explanation.walkthrough: Take AT out of AEROBATICS to leave AEROBICS. 'At' looks like a preposition joining the clue but is the letters to remove.
explanation.definitionFit: Aerobics is a programme of rhythmic workouts designed to raise heart rate and improve fitness.

clue.text: Ahead of rival, the ways German poet pens start of sonnet in time please

indicators.note: to be ahead of is to come before, so the following pieces precede the next one

parts.note: how means the way or manner in which

indicators.note: to pen is to shut in an enclosure, so one piece surrounds another

parts.note: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, author of Faust

indicators.note: the start of a word is its opening letter alone

parts.note: the opening letter of sonnet
a rival is an opponent or enemy

explanation.surface: A German poet writes a sonnet ahead of a rival, racing against the clock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'How goes the enemy?' is a jocular old way of asking the time, time being the enemy; 'the ways' stands for how, as in 'the ways it is done'.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a dated humorous request for the hour, popularised by Dickens, treating time as the foe.

clue.text: Crafty: can it work at first, being in debt?

parts.note: 'can it!' means be quiet, which is sh

indicators.note: something being inside another thing is enclosed by it

parts.note: in the red means in debt

indicators.note: 'at first' points to the opening letter of the word before it

parts.note: the initial letter of work

explanation.surface: A cunning debtor wonders whether a can of something might earn some money at first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Can it' reads like a question about a tin; it is the order to shut up. Being in the red, a debit balance, is the usual crossword route to debt.
explanation.definitionFit: Crafty and shrewd are synonyms, both describing someone clever and astute in practical dealings.

clue.text: Like the sea? Nothing bobs up in it, surprisingly

indicators.note: in a down clue, something that comes up reads from bottom to top
one piece placed in another sits inside it
a surprising result is an unexpected one, so the letters come out in an unexpected order

parts.note: 'it' refers back to the sea already named in the clue
nil means nothing

explanation.surface: A puzzled bather finds that nothing floats in the sea.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'it' points back to the sea of the definition, whose letters are rearranged to SAE around NIL upturned. The definition doubles as the source of the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Seawater is salty, and saline means containing or resembling salt in solution.

clue.text: Fabulous flyer missing end of crag

indicators.note: missing its end means the last letter has dropped off

parts.note: a crag is a steep rock

explanation.surface: A legendary bird has lost its way off the edge of a cliff.
explanation.walkthrough: ROCK loses its final K. 'Fabulous' means from fable, not marvellous.
explanation.definitionFit: The roc is a giant mythical bird from Arabian legend, appearing in the Sinbad tales.

clue.text: Wild arrow loosed in major conflict

indicators.note: letters that are loosed are set free from their order and can fall anywhere

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A stray arrow is fired during a great battle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wild' looks like the anagram signal, but it is part of the fodder; 'loosed' does that job, fitting an arrow released from a bow.
explanation.definitionFit: The Great War of 1914 to 1918 was among the largest wars in history, involving most major powers.

clue.text: Style of emperor, short on staff

indicators.note: something short has been cut, so its final letter goes
placed on means set beside, so one piece follows the other

parts.note: to staff a post is to man it
the Roman emperor who supposedly fiddled while Rome burned

explanation.surface: An emperor's style was to be short with his staff.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Staff' is a verb here, not the employees it seems, and 'short' trims the emperor rather than describing his temper.
explanation.definitionFit: Style and manner both mean the way in which something is done or a person behaves.

clue.text: Free entry to Wimbledon? Has it any value?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a place in a tournament given to a player who has not qualified
second meaning: a playing card that can stand for any other

explanation.walkthrough: The second question reads as doubt about the worth of the free pass, but it describes a card that may take any value. Wimbledon is the London tennis championship.
explanation.definitionFit: Organisers hand out wild cards to unqualified players, and in card games a wild card substitutes for whichever card its holder chooses.

clue.text: Even I can make a snowman

parts.note: even and yet both intensify, as in 'even/yet more'
taken as written

explanation.surface: A boast that even this speaker can build a figure out of snow.
explanation.walkthrough: The snowman is not a garden figure but the Abominable Snowman of the Himalayas.
explanation.definitionFit: The yeti is also called the Abominable Snowman, a legendary ape-like creature of the Himalayas.

clue.text: Have room next to brother for meditation

indicators.note: being next to means standing side by side, so pieces are joined in a row

parts.note: BR is the abbreviation for brother
to have something is to own it
a study is a room for reading and writing

explanation.surface: A monk asks for a room beside his brother's for his quiet contemplation.
explanation.walkthrough: The brother's abbreviation comes first in the answer though named last in the clue. 'Have room' is not about space but owning a room.
explanation.definitionFit: A brown study is an idiom for a state of deep absorbed thought or reverie.

clue.text: Different leaders take own groups in city

indicators.note: leaders go in front, so the opening letters of words are taken

parts.note: the first letter of take
taken as written
and then a different leading letter, G, for the same word again
the same word repeated, now behind its other leader

explanation.surface: Rival gang bosses each take charge of their own groups in the city.
explanation.walkthrough: OWN is used twice with different leading letters, T and G, giving TOWN and GOWN. Town and gown are the residents and the university members of a city like Oxford or Cambridge.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names the two traditional communities of a university city, locals versus academics, often at odds.

clue.text: Funds in an instant old woman provided for backing

indicators.note: something backing goes in reverse, so the assembled letters run backwards

parts.note: sec is short for second, an instant
nan is an informal word for grandmother
provided that means if

explanation.surface: Granny offers to put up money in a moment if backing is needed.
explanation.walkthrough: SEC, NAN and IF are strung together and the whole string read backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Funds and finances are synonyms, both meaning the money resources available to a person or body.

clue.text: Like a trespasser, confusing sin with virtue

indicators.note: to confuse things is to mix them up, scrambling their order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A trespasser with a muddled moral sense, mistaking wrongdoing for goodness.
explanation.walkthrough: The moral surface hides a plain jumble of both words.
explanation.definitionFit: A trespasser enters where not invited, and intrusive describes such unwelcome entering or imposing.

clue.text: Stole whiskey, facing charge

indicators.note: facing means set opposite and next to, so the pieces sit side by side

parts.note: whiskey is W in the NATO phonetic alphabet
a rap is a criminal charge, as in 'beat the rap'

explanation.surface: Someone pinched the whisky and now faces prosecution.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stole' looks like a past-tense verb but is the noun, a scarf.
explanation.definitionFit: A stole is a long scarf worn over the shoulders, a kind of wrap.

clue.text: Aim to break old soldier — army's vicious campaign

indicators.note: breaking into something means entering its middle, so one piece goes inside

parts.note: vet is short for veteran
an end is a goal or aim
TA is the Territorial Army, Britain's reserve force

explanation.surface: A veteran is targeted by his own army in a nasty smear campaign.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's of army's means 'has' and simply attaches the army abbreviation; the Territorial Army is Britain's volunteer reserve.
explanation.definitionFit: A vendetta is a prolonged bitter feud or persecution, a sustained campaign of hostility against someone.

clue.text: Second most important road sign

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for second
top means foremost, most important

explanation.surface: A ranking of highway signs, naming the runner-up in importance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Second most important' reads as one ranking phrase, but it splits into S and TOP.
explanation.definitionFit: A stop sign is a traffic signal ordering drivers to halt completely at a junction.

clue.text: Ancient script's inconsistent, grammar finally failing after the greeting

indicators.note: coming after means following in sequence

parts.note: hi is an informal greeting

indicators.note: something failing is going missing, so that letter drops out
finally picks out the last letter of the word before it as the one to drop

parts.note: erratic means irregular or inconsistent
the final letter of grammar, which is removed

explanation.surface: An old manuscript is patchy, its grammar falling apart after the opening salutation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Inconsistent' has a double R, and only one of them goes. 'Failing' reads as a judgment on the grammar but is the instruction to drop its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Hieratic was a cursive form of hieroglyphics used by ancient Egyptian priests for writing.

clue.text: Packed away as a precaution

definitions.meaning: first meaning: stored inside a container
second meaning: so as to be ready should something happen

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as one action, stowing something just in case, but the phrase is defined twice over.
explanation.definitionFit: Literally, contained in a box or holder; idiomatically, used adverbially to mean as a safeguard against a possibility.

clue.text: A month back, sounded off about the end of Europe being certain

indicators.note: going back means travelling the other way, so the letters run in reverse

parts.note: Aug is the short form of August

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece goes round another

parts.note: to sound off is to rant

indicators.note: the end of a word is its last letter

parts.note: the final letter of Europe

explanation.surface: Someone spent last month complaining about Europe's future being settled.
explanation.walkthrough: AUG is the calendar abbreviation for August; reversed it gives GUA. RANTED goes about E.
explanation.definitionFit: Guaranteed and certain are synonyms meaning sure to happen, assured beyond doubt.

clue.text: Parties needing hard cash

indicators.note: needing means wanting something added on, so another piece is joined

parts.note: dos are parties or social events
H is the abbreviation for hard, as on pencils

explanation.surface: Political parties needing hard cash to fight a campaign.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Parties' suggests politics, but it means celebrations, dos. Dosh is British slang for money.
explanation.definitionFit: Dosh is informal British slang for money, the ready cash in one's pocket.

clue.text: Mark, there's only one time for heart pill

indicators.note: leaving only one of a pair means its duplicate is taken away

parts.note: statins are drugs taken to lower cholesterol and protect the heart
T is the abbreviation for time; one of these is removed

explanation.surface: A note that a heart tablet is to be taken just once a day.
explanation.walkthrough: STATIN has two Ts; keeping only one gives STAIN. The surface reads like dosage instructions.
explanation.definitionFit: A mark and a stain are both a blemish or discoloured spot left on a surface.

clue.text: Chess among others independent school introduced to me

indicators.note: being introduced to is being brought into, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: taken as written
a gam is a school of whales
IND is the abbreviation for independent

explanation.surface: Someone recalls being taught chess and other games at a private school.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Independent school' looks like a private school but splits in two; gam is an obscure word for a school of whales.
explanation.definitionFit: Chess is one example of a game of strategy played purely by thought, alongside others such as go.

clue.text: Travel down at first, then up, to keep following

indicators.note: coming at first means placed at the front, before what follows

parts.note: D is the abbreviation for down

indicators.note: in a vertical entry, going up means reading from the bottom, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: to go is to travel

explanation.surface: A journey that goes down first and then back up again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At first' places D before the upturned GO. The words seem to describe a road; they are instructions.
explanation.definitionFit: To dog someone is to trail or track them persistently, as a hound pursues quarry.

clue.text: Beyond repair? I don't care

definitions.meaning: first meaning: so damaged that nothing can mend it
second meaning: a dismissive retort, tough luck

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as a shrug at something broken; the first phrase is literal, the second the dismissive idiom.
explanation.definitionFit: Literally, in excessively poor condition; as an exclamation, an unsympathetic shrug meaning tough luck or so what.

clue.text: Sue the French about a dog

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece is placed round another

parts.note: to sue is to plead or petition, like begging
taken as written
le is French for the

explanation.surface: Taking French people to court over a dog.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sue' suggests a lawsuit, but it has the older sense of plead or entreat.
explanation.definitionFit: The beagle is a small hound breed originally bred for hunting hares by scent.

clue.text: Deep desire to be studying with new head

indicators.note: giving something a new head swaps its first letter for a different one

parts.note: studying means learning; its first letter is replaced

explanation.surface: A strong wish to be back at school under a new headteacher.
explanation.walkthrough: LEARNING has its L swapped for Y; the clue does not say which new letter, so crossers must supply it. 'New head' looks like a school's head teacher.
explanation.definitionFit: Yearning is an intense longing, a deep wish for something out of reach.
